blocks.heading: Assisting businesses
blocks.text: Government can assist regional development, small firms and exports through grants, subsidies, tax allowances, low-interest loans, cheap or serviced premises, infrastructure, advice, training and information about markets. Regional support may address uneven opportunities; small firms may lack information or collateral; exporters may face unfamiliar customers and procedures. Assistance has an opportunity cost and can support weak projects if poorly targeted. Identify the actual constraint and conditions rather than assume a subsidy guarantees survival. Training may be on-the-job or off-the-job; choose it to address a capability gap rather than substitute for absent demand.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omi Crafts has good products but lacks reliable information about nearby regional buyers and delivery options. Relevant market and logistics advice may address its gap more directly than an unneeded machine grant. The firm must still confirm demand and affordability.

blocks.heading: Regional assistance
blocks.text: Regional assistance supports areas with limited economic opportunities through suitable infrastructure, advice, skills or conditional financial support. It can encourage productive activity and employment, but needs a realistic reason firms can operate there. Public cost and the risk of temporary relocation matter. Measure enduring outcomes rather than buildings or grant totals alone.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A region has willing workers and demand access but lacks a reliable industrial electricity connection. Improving that connection can remove a stated obstacle. A marketing campaign about the region would not supply the missing utility.

blocks.heading: Assistance to small firms
blocks.text: Small firms can face limited finance, management time, information and access to specialist support. Government assistance can include advice, relevant development opportunities, suitable premises or eligible funding. Match it to the specific weakness and check whether demand and operations are viable. Support does not eliminate business risk or establish a right to indefinite subsidy.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eya Repairs has customers and skills but weak cash planning. Practical financial-planning advice can help identify payment timing and avoid an unaffordable commitment. An unrelated equipment grant may not address the problem.

blocks.heading: Assistance to exporters
blocks.text: Government helps exporters because exports earn foreign currency that pays for imports, create jobs, and raise tax revenue from exporters’ profits. It can help by offering low-interest loans, subsidies or tax reductions to exporters, insuring exporters against foreign buyers who do not pay, organising trade fairs and trade missions abroad, providing market information and advice about foreign requirements, and trying to keep the exchange rate stable. It can reduce information barriers but cannot guarantee foreign orders or remove all transport and payment risk. Exporting services may involve different access and delivery arrangements from sending physical goods. Confirm the opportunity and costs before committing.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ota Crafts considers a nearby regional market but does not know buyer requirements or delivery costs. Market and logistics information helps assess suitability. A large export target without those details would be a weak basis for investment.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Assistance to producers and trade implications
blocks.text:
Hela Crafts in Namibia has spare capacity and an offering potentially suitable for regional buyers. It lacks market and delivery information. An assistance programme can provide advice and contacts; another offers unneeded extra equipment. Relevant trade preferences have conditions, and no current tariff rate is supplied.

a(i) State two ways government can assist a producer. [2]
a(ii) State one potential regional-trade opportunity and one risk for Namibia. [2]
b State two reasons government may assist businesses. [2]
c Explain whether advice or extra equipment better addresses Hela’s constraint. [6]
d Evaluate using regional trading opportunities as a reason for Hela to export immediately. [8]

a(i) Relevant market advice and usable infrastructure. a(ii) Wider potential markets and stronger import competition. b Supporting regional development and employment. c Spare capacity means extra machines do not address the known gap. Advice and contacts can supply buyer and logistics evidence, helping Hela assess delivered cost and demand. Assistance is worthwhile if relevant, though it still uses resources and needs review. d Regional access can provide opportunities but preferences are conditional and buyers still require suitable products and delivery. Hela lacks information, so immediate substantial export commitment is unjustified. Use advice and verify a feasible trial first; membership alone does not create orders or eliminate trade barriers.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Assistance to producers and trade implications
blocks.text:
Hela Crafts in Namibia has spare capacity and an offering potentially suitable for regional buyers. It lacks market and delivery information. An assistance programme can provide advice and contacts; another offers unneeded extra equipment. Relevant trade preferences have conditions, and no current tariff rate is supplied.

a Explain how assistance should address Hela’s constraint and what limits should be recognised. [8]
b Evaluate the implications of regional trading opportunities for a producer and consumers in Namibia. [12]

a Market and delivery advice supplies missing evidence while existing spare capacity can serve a verified opportunity. Equipment support might add idle resources and public cost without solving access. Advice quality and actual demand still require assessment; neither programme guarantees sales. b Producers may gain wider markets and input choices, while consumers may gain variety and competitive prices. Local firms also face stronger rivals, possible loss of sales and adjustment for workers. Preferences depend on applicable arrangements and qualifying conditions, not simply a SADC label. Namibia’s benefits therefore depend on firms’ capability, logistics and responses as well as market access. Support competitiveness and informed participation while assessing affected groups; do not claim every producer or consumer gains equally.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Assistance to producers and trade implications
blocks.text:
Nara Panels in Namibia has suitable spare capacity, dependable delivery options and verified interest from eligible regional buyers at a feasible delivered price. It compares a limited regional export trial with staying solely local, using available market-information support. For part (b) only, reliable transport becomes unavailable so the required regional delivery deadline cannot be met. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Nara’s trial under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate it after the transport constraint changes. Explain whether the original recommendation holds. [12]

a A limited trial uses existing capacity and verified market interest with feasible delivery, while retaining caution about competition and payment. Information support can help, but the producer remains responsible for assessing actual terms. Prefer the trial over an unnecessary permanent commitment. b The required deadline is now impossible with stated transport, so the original logistics condition fails. Postpone or renegotiate the trial and investigate a reliable alternative before accepting orders. Regional preferences and buyer interest do not physically deliver goods. The recommendation changes because access is no longer feasible, while the potential regional opportunity remains worth investigating.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Assistance to producers and trade implications
blocks.text:
Nara Panels in Namibia has suitable spare capacity, dependable delivery options and verified interest from eligible regional buyers at a feasible delivered price. It compares a limited regional export trial with staying solely local, using available market-information support.

Evaluate Nara’s limited regional trial against remaining solely local. Give a concise plan. [12]

Opportunity: verified interest, feasible delivered price, spare capacity and dependable logistics support a controlled trial. Assistance: use relevant information and check applicable preference conditions. Risks: competition, payment and dependence on a new market remain. Alternative: local-only focus avoids some complexity but forgoes the evidenced opportunity. Judgement: try a limited export commitment and monitor paid demand, costs and service; regional membership is an enabling context rather than a guarantee.
